utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will be leading Dr. Donia in evidence. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have the documents SK1 to SK41 as exhibits. Then we have the report that was filed the 22nd of March, and additionally, you provided us with the transcripts. utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That's my perfect understand. Dr. Donia, in fact, his testimony will simply be an abridged version of the 20-page report. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then Dr. Donia may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One last matter, Mr. President. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Please, Mr. Cayley, take care yourself when you regard it as necessary to have the break after -- yes, it should be somewhere at 10.30, the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's up to you how to conduct this. And then Dr. Donia may come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Donia. Please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Donia. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before we commence, I know you've testified a number of times before the Tribunal before, but if you can remember that we both speak the same language. There are interpreters between us, so I will be listening to the French translation and I will be pausing after your answers to allow the translation to catch up. First of all, Dr. Donia, very briefly, if you could tell Their Honours something of your antecedents, your academic credentials, why you are qualified to give an expert opinion before this Court.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I first spent time in the former Yugoslavia in the mid-1970s, 1974, 1975, on a Fulbright Hayes grant doing research for dissertation in history at the University of Michigan that dealt with the Bosnian Muslims in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. I subsequently completed that dissertation at the University of Michigan in 1976 and taught at Ohio State University Lima campus and the University of Oregon for four years, at which time I left the academic profession and worked for the firm of Merrill Lynch in matters completely unrelated to south-eastern Europe from 1981 until 1998. I have since then conducted research and writing and lectured on matters dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, and I currently have an appointment as a research scholar at the University of California at San Diego and as a research associate at the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if the letter of request could be handed out to the Court and Their Honours, and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I'm handing to you the letter that was written to you by Ms. Korner, which sets out the requirements of the Office of the Prosecutor in respect of your expert opinion, both in written form and your oral testimony today. Can you explain to the Judges very briefly what was required of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I was asked to examine documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, and on the basis of those, to prepare a report on the factors which may have contributed to the events in Prijedor from 1992 to 1995 -- I'm sorry, April 1992 to December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you have a binder in front of you which are the exhibits which Their Honours have in front of them, marked SK1 to SK41. Can you very briefly explain the contents of this file?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The vast majority of the documentation in this binder consists of one of two things: First is an extensive set of minutes from the meetings of the Prijedor SDS Main Board in 1991 and the first half of 1992. Most of the other exhibits pertain to our press articles taken primarily from the local Prijedor newspaper Vjesnik in the same time period. There are also a few documents which were -- which are in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor which are declarations or decisions by local bodies in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, the Prijedor SDS Main Board minutes are, I believe, Exhibit 12A and 12B in the binder. Can you very briefly explain to the Judges exactly what those minutes are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These minutes exist in one bound volume in the original language, are handwritten in Cyrillic script, and are divided into, perhaps as many as 30 meetings held principally by the Prijedor SDS Main Board, and a few meetings held by other bodies which were related to the SDS Main Board. One for example, of the club of deputies of the SDS in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. There is also the English translation of those minutes which precedes it. The handwriting is clearly taken at times in haste, and so there are many incomplete sentences, and in some instances reference that are not wholly clear, but by and large it represents the deliberations and debates that went on in the Prijedor SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, these minutes, they are not a transcript of what was stated; they are simply a summary of what was stated by the various participants in these meetings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct. They are secretaries' minutes as transcription of the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, very briefly, referring to the principal report that you produced for Brdjanin and Talic, in that report you refer to what you regard as the three most significant events which in your opinion preceded the war in the former Yugoslavia. Could you very briefly explain to the Judges those three significant events.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In that report I identified three important factors which preceded the Bosnian war. Number 1 was the collapse of the communist -- or League of Communists of Yugoslavia in January 1990. Number 2 was the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the latter half of the twentieth century. Those elections were held in November, November 18th, 1990. And third was the decennial census which was taken at the end of March 1991 throughout the former Yugoslavia, and in each municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that these three particular events did have a special effect on the events in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the multiparty elections that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in November of 1990. Can you explain to the Judges who the principal political parties were that were participants in those multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The three parties that won the most votes were the three principal nationalist parties, namely, the Croatian Democratic Union, or HDZ, which represented Croatian voters; the Serbian Democratic Party, or SDS, a party of Serbs; and the Party of Democratic Action, or SDA, which was the Bosnian Muslim political party. Together, these parties won something over 80 per cent of the votes and positions in the voting of November 1990, and between them, among them, controlled the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the executive organ for which elections were held. The so-called opposition parties were numerous. The two primary vote-getters among the opposition parties were the League of Communists Social Democratic Party, which was the formerly ruling League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had changed its name and adopted the additional title of Social Democratic Party in the months before the election. The second party that won a good number of votes was the Alliance of Reformist Forces of Yugoslavia. This party was founded by Yugoslavia federal prime minister Ante Markovic and favoured economic reforms. Markovic was a Serb -- or a Croat from Bosnia, and selected as the place to inaugurate the party's activities Mount Kozara just above Prijedor because of the important historical association of that location with the Partisan resistance in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll come on to that subject very briefly, Dr. Donia. Now, you stated that these multiparty elections took place at a national level. Did they also take place at a local level in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. They took place in each of the 109 municipalities, where voting took place for the Municipal Assembly of each municipality, and these municipalities -- the assemblies were typically sizeable. They ranged in size from 27 members to 130. So the municipalities themselves had a sizeable ruling bodies which were these assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with a map which was I think offered by Ms. Korner yesterday. Mr. President, I've given it, if I may, an exhibit number, 48. It's a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you could place it on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, very briefly, if you could explain to the Judges the structure of the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You've already referred to it that there was a government at a national level and then at a municipal level.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In 1990, the character of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could you please provide that we can also see the map on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the machine, Your Honour, is warming up at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the power is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the power could be switched on the projector. Your Honours, can you now -- you can see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of six republics in the socialist federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As with the other republics, Bosnia and Herzegovina was administratively divided into municipalities or opstina. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1990, there were 109 such municipalities. In most cases, they were rural administrative units centred on a town of some size, either smaller or larger, after which the municipality was named. In some cases, these municipalities cooperated in associations for particular purposes, school districts, economic cooperation, matters like that, but the municipalities had been the primary administrative unit under various names, dating back over a hundred years. So the practice of these local administrative units was one that had persisted over the decades, really, of the twentieth century. Prijedor, of course, is one municipality in the north-western part of Bosnia, a part of the area known as the Bosnian Krajina because of its historical role as a border land from the time of the Ottoman Empire prior to 1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, you've already stated to Their Honours that the main victors of the multiparty elections were the nationally-based parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. In your principal report for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brdjanin and Talic, you refer to the inter parte agreement, which I know from your report on Prijedor has an important effect on matters in Prijedor. Can you explain to Their Honours exactly what the inter party agreement was and how it affected the allocation of positions of authority at both national and municipal levels.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: During the election campaign, the three national parties formed an informal agreement among themselves not to attack one another, and rather, to direct all their campaigning activities against the incumbent League of Communists, social Democrats, and other non-national parties. This agreement was informal. It was largely honoured throughout the campaign, although not in all municipalities and not at all times. And assured that the three national parties did not detract from one another's appeal, particularly in municipalities with roughly balanced populations between the nationalities. As the election approached and the prospect of a victory by these parties became more likely, the Republican-level party leaders extended that inter-party agreement to the division of primary positions in government, should they be victorious, and after the election, this agreement was further extended to an agreement regarding numerous portfolios within the government. The primary provision was that the first vote-getting party would be entitled to the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly; the second party would appoint the president of the executive committee of the municipality, and the third party -- or the first party again would get the vice-presidency of the Municipal Assembly. And this agreement pertained to a number of portfolios within the municipality. The police was perhaps the most important of these portfolios in Prijedor, and the inter-party agreement provided that the chief of police would be designated by the first vote-getting party. His second in command, who was referred to as the commander of the police station, would be designated by the second vote-getting party. And the commander of the traffic police would go also to the first vote-getting party in the municipality. This had various iterations according to the national -- the party leaders who reached it, and its application in both the republic-level government and municipalities was the primary source of political contention in the first months after the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, we will speak about the details of Prijedor and the contention that took place there in 1991 and 1992 in a moment. Now, one or two other matters from your main report. You refer to the concept of regionalisation within the report that you produced for the Brdjanin and Talic case, and that is relevant to events in Prijedor. Can you explain to the Judges the concept of regionalisation and the effect that that concept had on matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Regionalisation was a concept that was promoted principally, although not exclusively, by the SDS. It consisted of three different strategies or approaches. The first and most obvious form of regionalisation was the creation of a body made up of several municipalities which had a majority Serbian population, or a substantial Serbian population. So these regional associations was the first variant. The second form of regionalisation was the creation of new municipalities with Serb-majority population, created by carving out those Serbian territories from existing municipalities. And the third concept was to create parallel institutions, parallel to the elected ruling institutions of existing municipalities, without a necessarily territorial designation assigned to those institutions. These were all concepts adopted by the SDS from earlier precedents, and at times were advocated by the HDZ, the Croatian party, as well as the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the SDA, or the Muslim party, engage in regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The SDA did engage in very limited efforts to organise separate Muslim institutions in three or four municipalities in Bosnia, principally in reaction to regionalisation efforts by other national parties. It was generally, however, opposed to the regional breakdown of Bosnia-Herzegovina and instead supported a unified republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, another subject addressed at some length in your main report. I want to also address this very briefly. The JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, how was that army connected with the state of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, was born as the Partisans of Josip Broz Tito in World War II. It carefully nurtured and guarded that revolutionary partisan tradition. It was the army of Yugoslavia and was tasked by constitutional mandate both to defend the country against external aggression and to protect the socialist order of Yugoslavia. It therefore was a key institution in keeping Yugoslavia together, and after the collapse of the League of Communists in January 1990 was the principal institution holding Yugoslavia together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the organisation of the Territorial Defence has relevance to events in Prijedor. Can you explain to the Judges what the Territorial Defence was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Coming out of the World War II partisan experience, Yugoslav defence theory emphasised that there needed to be a local force, local individual -- local forces that could respond rapidly in the event of any outside invasion or threat and be made up principally of local volunteers. Consequently, the Territorial Defence forces, or TO, were an integral part of Yugoslav defence theory. In the 1970s, local TO organisations came under the administration of the ministries of defence of the individual republics, in addition to being a part of the JNA command structure, and the theory was that they would hold off and could hold off in isolation any outside invader until such time as the JNA could become effective in driving an invader out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let us now move to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown appendix 2 of his report, which is a map, an extract of a map showing Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if you could identify firstly the significant geographical features on this map and then identify for Their Honours the strategic importance of Prijedor, the city of Prijedor and the municipality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The dominant physical feature in Prijedor is the mountain range that runs along that northern part of the municipality, and I believe we can see this dotted line which defines the area known as the Mount Kozara National Park. This is a series of summits rather than a single high summit, but the two most important ones are Mrakovica, right here, which is the site of a large partisan monument, and Lisina, which is right here, the site of an important television relay station in northern -- north-western Bosnia. This highland contrasts with the long valley to its south-east, and through that valley runs a road and a railroad line which connect Banja Luka to the north-western part of the rest of Bosnia, and also the Croatian territories beyond Bosanski Novi. And these had great strategic significance in World War II and in the period of the 1990s for their role in connecting those two areas. The other area of considerable significance is the large iron mine at Ljubija. In World War II, this was a very valuable resource that at various times both the occupying forces and the Partisans exploited for its iron ore potential and continued to be a very -- really, I think, the keystone of the Prijedor municipality economy throughout the socialist period, from 1945 to 1990. Within this, of course, is the city of Prijedor, which has always been an important intersection between this east/west road and the route running further north into the mountains and into Croatia, and also the administrative centre of this area and itself the location of some local industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you referred a moment ago to the strategic significance of this area during the Second World War, and I know in your report you link events during the Second World War with events that took place in the early 1990s, so I think it would be prudent for a moment to refer to those events. Firstly, within the area of Prijedor and the Krajina, who were the principal protagonists during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Prijedor municipality, as the rest -- like the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was conquered in April 1941 by German forces, and with some help from Italians, and in Zagreb, the extreme nationalist -- Croatian nationalist Ustasha regime was put in authority all over -- most of Croatia and nearly all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Consequently, this area came under both German and Italian and Ustasha administration. In the early months of Ustasha rule, north-western Bosnia was the scene of many massacres carried out by Ustasha units and bands and their allies, directed against Serbs, Jews, and Romany, and even Croats who opposed the regime. Many thousands of Serbs were killed, by far the most numerous victims of these activities were Serbs. And many others were sent to concentration camps, the best known of which and most important of which was the Jasenovac concentration camp, which was very close to Prijedor, just across the river in Croatia, directly to the north of Prijedor town. And so this -- these atrocities and ongoing slaughters evoked a rebellion which began as a Serbian rebellion against these Ustasha atrocities and became part of the partisan resistance movement which was led by Josip Broz Tito. In 1942, the partisans actually captured the city of Prijedor in May 1942, and this and other successes led the German High Command to order a major offensive against Eastern Bosnia and north-western Bosnia in which became known in socialist literature as the Third Enemy Offensive. This offensive was successful in that the Germans recaptured Prijedor and took control of the Ljubija mine and encircled a large partisan force on Mount Kozara. But they were not able to completely exterminate that force and some partisans escaped the encirclement, and this became a staple of the story of partisan heroism and the Yugoslav revolutionary successes, partisan successes, that were celebrated in the times of socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown appendix 5 to his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated in your final sentence, Dr. Donia, that the successes of the partisans was celebrated in socialist Yugoslavia, and I think appendix 5 from your report represents a part of that celebration. If you could explain to the Judges the nature of that photograph and where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I took this picture in October of last year on Mount Kozara, at Mrakovica. This monument was built in the early 1970s as a memorial to the partisan victims and those civilians who perished in this area. And to the left of this monument is an area, a very excluded area in the woods, with the embossed names of over 9.000 victims or people who died -- partisans who died in these battles. This became really something of a shrine visited by school students and also became -- they designated this entire area the national park, as I indicated before, and the national park issued publications and held meetings to the right of this memorial, about 300 yards, is a hotel complex and meeting centre, and it's just to the right of this memorial that Ante Markovic held his organising meeting of the Alliance of Reformist Forces of Yugoslavia in July of 1990. So this became a memorial that was widely known and honoured in socialist Yugoslavia. The name Kozara became the name of a military barracks, the newspaper in Prijedor adopted that name, Kozarski Vjesnik, and the military war unit of the Territorial Defence forces was known as the Fifth Kozara Brigade. So the name Kozara came to embody this revolutionary tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in conclusion, the fact that these terrible atrocities had been committed in Prijedor and the fact that it had been a centre of this heroic partisan resistance, did this have an effect on events in 1990 and onwards into 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the partisan tradition was more powerful, more durable, in Prijedor municipality than many other places in Bosnia, and it explains in part the relatively successful performance of the League of Communists, Social Democrats, and Reformists in the elections of November 1990, because in Prijedor itself, the election results gave 30 seats in the Municipal Assembly to the SDA, the Muslim party; 28 seats to the SDS, the Serbian party; and 30 seats to the combined Reformists, social Democrats, and a couple of other small parties, one other small party. Consequently, Prijedor was one of the few municipalities in which the so-called Left Bloc, or opposition, played a significant political role after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, on page 1 of your report, you identify four factors which had a particular effect on events in Prijedor from January 1990. Now, you've already identified one of those, the Partisan legacy, which you've just spoken about. What were the other three factors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, first was the relationship, demographic relationship, between Serbs and Muslims. For the entire twentieth century, the Serbs had enjoyed a demographic plurality or majority in Prijedor, but in the 1991 census, these two groups were neck and neck, and the Muslims, in terms of census respondents, had a few more than the Serbs for the first time in the twentieth century. That was one factor. The important role of the non-nationalist or leftist parties was another factor. It meant that in the Municipal Assembly, no single party could accomplish anything without the support and cooperation of one other party or group. And the last factor I've identified was an unusually contentious SDS organisation in the first year of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you've already stated to the Court the results of the multiparty elections in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly in 1990. Now, speaking again about the inter-party agreement, was this implemented in the municipality of Prijedor between the three nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The inter-party agreement was implemented in the early months after the election between the SDS and the SDA. The SHDZ's claims were largely ignored, but those two parties, after difficult and long negotiations, agreed upon about the top dozen, say 10 to 15 appointments in the city government, in the municipal government. And at its first meeting in the 1991 year, in January, the SDS and SDA agreed on the key appointments, six top appointments, of which I'll just name three: The president of the Municipal Assembly per the inter-party agreement was nominated by the SDA, and that was Muhamed Cehajic; the president of the executive committee was Milan Kovacevic, nominated by the SDS; and the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, also designated by the SDS, was Dr. Milomir Stakic. And then the subsequent three positions were likewise divided between those two parties, so that they were three and three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that that information is contained in a Kozarski Vjesnik article behind tab 2, Exhibit 2 in the exhibits in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, Exhibits 2 to 8 in the binder are also newspaper articles from Kozarski Vjesnik, and they in essence give us a snapshot of the first six months of the functioning of the Municipal Assembly after the multiparty elections. Can you briefly summarise for the Judges what happened in those first six months. I think you've already started in terms of explaining the election of various officials, but can you go on from that period, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Assembly sessions were long, tortuous, and centred primarily on the adoption of the agenda. However, the assembly was successful in addressing a number of burning issues facing the municipality. There were several strikes that were settled with the assistance of the municipal leadership. Additional portfolios beyond the six that I mentioned were agreed upon at the second session of the assembly, but further negotiations on the division of portfolios, governing portfolios and appointments between the SDS and the SDA were unsuccessful. They were ongoing and they were at times close to a resolution but never actually achieved an agreement on most positions. The assembly met approximately monthly, but it was -- many of its activities were in a sense frozen by the failure to agree on governing portfolios.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like to take a break at this point or do you want to continue for a while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's an appropriate moment, and we should resume at ten minutes to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we have Dr. Donia once again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. He's being fetched at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably it's just the time to decide whether or not we take the document filed the 22nd of March, the report of Dr. Donia, as such, as document P1, only the document, nothing about the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, quite. We would be offering it into evidence, but I think its number will be P -- SK42, the reason being that the first 1 to 41 are the documents that Dr. Donia is referring to. So that particular exhibit will be SK42A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there are no fundamental objections, both from the Defence and from the registry, we can proceed as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the report -- the major report done on the Bosnian Krajina will be SK43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now it's a kind of attachment to this report; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit hard, Your Honour, to represent it by that, because it is the major component. The report for this case was a subsidiary report, but the evidence contained within it is relevant and is material to this case. So we've marked it as a separate exhibit, 43. It follows on directly from the Prijedor report, which is 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be the part 1997 24PT page 10.788 on the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Then this should be SK43; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But already today I'll ask the Office of the Prosecutor to show, probably next week, after the hearing of Dr. Donia, for additional good cause why it should be necessary to introduce the transcripts of Brdjanin and Talic in this case, because until now we can't see any additional value.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't want to hear argument on that now, Your Honour; you want to hear argument on that later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I decided yesterday that we should discuss this the 24th, taking into account that it's right to have seven days for the Defence to prepare any kind of objection. So therefore, this should be discussed not earlier than 24 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before the break we were speaking about the first six months of the functioning of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor, and I want you to now focus on the summer of 1991 and the disagreement between the SDS and the SDA over the appointment of senior officials within the police department in Prijedor. If you could explain to the Judges. You've referred to it briefly already, but if you could explain what exactly happened in respect of that disagreement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: As I indicated, the inter-party agreement provided for the leading vote-getting party, the SDA, to get the first and third positions in the police department. In summer 1991, the SDS made its nomination known for the position of commander of the police station, the number-two position. However, the republican government, the ministry of internal affairs, which has responsibility for the police, judged this candidate to be unqualified to serve as commander of the police station. Consequently, he was not put in office, and after negotiations between the two parties, a Muslim nominee was placed in that position for an interim period of two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this matter, the appointment of the second-ranking police officer, ever resolved between the SDS and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think this particular event is referred to on page 5 of your report and in Exhibits 8 to 10 of the bundle of documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, let's move now to page 6 of your report, and let us speak of the Prijedor SDS. When was the Prijedor SDS founded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: August of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think that date comes from the minutes of the SDS board of the 3rd of July of 1991, and I'm going to direct your attention to that in a moment. You stated that one of the factors that influenced the municipality of Prijedor was the very fractious intra-party relationships within the SDS, and I think in your report you refer to a meeting of the 3rd of July of 1991 to demonstrate and support that opinion. And if I can now direct you to that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will find that behind tab 12 of the bundle, as part of the SDS party municipal board minutes. In the bottom right-hand corner of this document there is an ERN number, which is the evidence registry number, and that is how I will assist you in navigating through these documents. If you refer to the last three digits, which you will see on the front of this document is 336, and if I can direct you to 369. So the whole number is in fact an eight-digit number, but I'm only referring to the last three digits. It's 369, and there you will find the minutes of the Prijedor SDS of the 3rd of July of 1991. Sorry, Your Honour. The Defence don't have these, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe we do. I don't know. But can you tell us first which binder? Because we've got four binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's the -- this is volume 1 of 1, Donja Exhibits SK1 to SK41, the documents related to the Prijedor report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please, one additional request: Whenever you want to go into details of this document, which evidently has not yet been translated into the French language, could you read it out. Then we have it in the transcript in French as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Just to clarify matters with the Defence, my understanding is that they were placed in the Defence locker yesterday, but we can actually give you another set if you don't have them in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We accept the offer by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you not write on that set, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you heard what His Honour Judge Schomburg said. If you could read slowly any of the sections which are of particular relevance. I know mainly you will summarise the essence of these meetings. This meeting of the 3rd of July of 1991, what was significant about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, let me first read, if I may, the title perhaps: "Minutes of the Meeting of the Assembly of the Prijedor SDS, 3 July 1991." This meeting was begun by Mr. Radomir Neskovic, who was a member of the Main Board of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was in this meeting acting as something of an overseer. Halfway down this first page, one sees him saying, Mr. Neskovic, member of the Main Board of the VHSDS was given the floor. He conveyed the greetings of the Main Board and suggested the following agenda: Number 1, performance report. And moving on to the second page, at the bottom of the second page of the English translation, we see that the four-item agenda that he proposed was in fact, in the last sentence, the agenda was adopted with one vote against, cast by Mr. Mijatovic, that's Mr. Mijatovic, who had no right to vote. So the role of Mr. Neskovic as the overseer of this is first of all directed toward requesting a performance report from the president of the Prijedor SDS, Mr. Srdic. I think that the request for a performance report is a universal organisational signal that one's performance is not up to standard. And in the performance report, Mr. Srdic gives a rather bland description of the party's activities up to this point. On the third page, top of the third page, with the section that begins performance report, the president of the Prijedor SDS municipal board submitted the report. The Prijedor SDS was established on 2 August 1990, on St. Alias day in Maricka. In the -- about six lines down, he notes that -- he says: "He also mentioned the division of power." This is a reference to the inter-party agreement, "and the celebration of Christmas Eve. The division of power at the municipal level came to a halt for objective reasons, the failure to meet the requirements of certain offices." This is a reference to the SDS nominee for the position of chief of the police station. Following this performance report, it is greeted by a torrent of criticism from other party members. About two-thirds of the way down the page, Zdravko Jovic states that there was not enough self-criticism in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report and there had been failures. The next paragraph he continues: "We only appointed eight people to the offices of the authority and in order to function we need at least 200 people." And moving to page 4 of this report, or the next page, the ERN last three digits being 372, we see Mr. Dusan Kurnuga, about one-third of the way down the page, Dusan Kurnuga objected to the misplaced applause and to the dual between Jovic and Srdic. He expressed that he was chiefly responsible for establishing an SDS chapter in Prijedor. Moving down four lines, he continues: "After Milakovic, a new group of people came to oust Milakovic, and now those same people were to be ousted. Electoral defeat happened because of the communist methods of work." Then down two brief paragraphs: "The performance report was not acceptable. It would have to be prepared differently. Difficulties in organising the party in the town of Prijedor." Onto the next page, the second speaker there, Mr. Milo Radetic, he was not satisfied with the report. And down two paragraphs, Mr. Mico Kovacevic, there has been no real takeover of power except in those departments which have been distributed so far. Now, these I think are all indications of the internal dissent and criticism of the leadership that are expressed at this meeting. And Mr. Milan Pilipovic, down two more speakers, begins to identify the key problems that these speakers see. His point 1 is the party must gain more support among the Serbs. 75 per cent of the Serbian population voted for the SDS." That number, of course, is far below the per cent in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. And on the following page - this is 374 - one-third of the way down, Mr. Momcilo Radanovic, recommendation to the Prijedor intellectuals to find a way for a larger area of the former Omarska municipality to separate from the Prijedor municipality and join the Banja Luka region. This is a reference to the regionalisation strategies then being considered by the party. So this meeting is evidence, I think, of substantial internal dissension in the party and a leadership crisis with the existing president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you stated that the figure of 75 per cent of the Serbian population in Prijedor voting for the SDS, and then you went on to say that that number, of course, is far below the per cent in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole. Are you stating that in Prijedor, the number of Serbs who voted for the SDS was significantly below those Serbs in other municipalities who voted for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of that particular issue, I think it had been addressed previously, and I want you to speak in more detail on that particular matter, the matter of Serbs voting for the SDS. And if we can now go to the meeting of the 20th of March of 1991, which, Your Honours, you will find on ERN number 343. Now, this particular meeting of the SDS municipal board I believe was held immediately prior to the population census; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, 11 days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in this particular set of minutes, they express some considerable concern about ensuring that all people of Serb ethnicity declare themselves as Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point to those particular sections and speakers who do express those concerns?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. If I can maybe read the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: "Meeting of the Prijedor SDS municipal board, 20 March 1991." The first and predominant item on the agenda is report and preparations for the census. This meeting, I think should be noted, is attended by a number of non-SDS members and is apparently an open, public discussion of the party's preparation for the census. On page 345, at the top of the page, there is a quote from Mr. Ecim, who has been giving the report on preparations for the census: "The general principle applied in census-taking is the territorial principle. The party can exert influence through the census committee and the instructors." Also on page 345, down three paragraphs: "It is a fact that the committee, almost all committees from the republican level down to the municipal one, is in the hands of Muslims. The counting of farming land units is more vital than the population census, because 69 per cent of the land is in Serbian hands." And moving to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could you explain to the Judges the significance of that particular comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there are two comments there, and one is, of course, the party's concern about who is controlling the census-taking process, and obviously it's a matter of concern and a negative that the Muslims are controlling those committees, in the view of Mr. Kursumovic. The second comment indicates a feeling that if the population figures turn out unfavourable, from the Serbian standpoint, they will nonetheless be concerned about what percentage of land in the municipality is controlled by -- is owned by Serbs. I can move to page 3, 4, it's almost illegible there, but it's 346. Toward the bottom of the page 346, Ecim. Ecim remarked that nationality is the most sensitive issue, Serb, Muslim, Croat, and others, which is a miscellaneous category "if someone states that he is an orthodox Christian, he will be included among others." This is a kind of warning that if one identifies himself only by religion, it would not necessarily put that person in the Serbian national category. The next paragraph: "Savanovic, insisting the absence of republican instructors, the problem is making the Serbs realise that they are of Serbian nationality and not Yugoslavs." His concern here is that those responding to the census will identify themselves as Yugoslavs and detract from the Serbian count. Next paragraph: "The solution, every local board to stage a panel and to convince people to declare themselves Serbs." And going on: "For the president, Srdic wanted a radio programme be arranged, the main point of which would be to appeal to the Serbs to say that they are Serbs." So in this meeting, the party is making extensive preparations to try to assure that everyone who ought to be counted in the census as a Serb is in fact so counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown appendix 4 of his report, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 42A.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying, Dr. Donia, that all of this discussion was taking place because the Serbs were very concerned in Prijedor that the Muslims were going to outnumber them after the population census had taken place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That was a concern not only in Prijedor municipality but throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a graph which you produced which indicates the numbers of the various ethnic groups within Prijedor from 1879 to 1991, and if you could explain to the Judges firstly where the information comes from to produce this graph, and secondly, the significance of the data that's represented.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared this chart using census returns from the Austro-Hungarian period, the Royal Yugoslav Period, and socialist Yugoslav period as well, and I think there's some caution I would note in the use of these numbers. The first three censuses are not considered by most observers to be particularly accurate, those of 1879 to 1895, and the categories for those first four censuses were in fact religion rather than nationality. Nevertheless, there is, over time, a consistency here that I think is well illustrated by this graph. Throughout the twentieth century, the Serbs held a numerical advantage in Prijedor municipality, and the Muslims, who are the green line, were rapidly gaining on that number in the years from 1961 onward. There is one curious fact here that should be noted, and that is that in 1953, one could not identify himself or herself as a Muslim by nationality. The only option available was -- or one of the options available was Yugoslav. And so many of those who declared themselves Muslims in 1948 or 1961 clearly in this situation opted for the Yugoslav identity. That number falls precipitously in 1961, the Yugoslavs, further in 1971, spikes up in 1981, and declines somewhat again in 1991. This was the group to which the members of the SDS referred in saying that they believed that many of these people who declared themselves Yugoslavs were in fact Serbs. The other group of interest, although not numerically very significant, was "others," and it was the concern of the SDS in 1991 that the "others" category included many people who ought to be declared Serbs. And it is in fact the case that either the Yugoslav or the "other" category, if added to the number of Serbs in the census, would have produced a Serbian relative majority in the 1991 census. The two combined, of course, would have produced a substantial increase in the number of Serbian respondents. So this became the focus of SDS activities, both before the census and immediately afterwards, when the SDS sent a letter to the census commission and asked for the census to be retaken in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what was the result of that request for the census to be taken again?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That request received no response.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you haven't already made it clear, this graph clearly shows that in 1991, on the basis of the census, for the first time since the nineteenth century, the Muslims were in the relative majority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's turn our attention, Dr. Donia, to the meeting of the 30th of April of 1991, which appears on page 348.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's the set of minutes, Your Honours, immediately after the meeting concerning the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think at this time, in April of 1991, the Prijedor SDS municipal board was concerned about becoming a member of the Krajina association of municipalities. Can you explain to the Judges what the Krajina association of municipalities was and how this relates to the concept of regionalisation, which you've already referred to in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In pursuit of a regional association of municipalities with substantial Serbian populations, a group of SDS leaders in north-western Bosnia convened a founding assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina on the 25th of April, 1991, in the town of Celinac. At that meeting, 14 municipalities had already voted to become charter members of the Krajina, what's called the ZOBK, the acronym for the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina. Prijedor was not one of those, but Prijedor SDS representatives were present at that meeting as guests, and this meeting of the SDS Prijedor municipal board held on 30 April 1991 reflects a report on that regionalisation meeting by, first of all, Mr. Pilipovic, and then other persons who were present at the meeting. The discussion then turns to the question of how the Prijedor municipality might join the ZOBK. Its dilemma was that the SDS, with only 28 votes in the Municipal Assembly, lacked the requisite votes to pass such a resolution in Prijedor. The solution that is agreed upon can be seen at the bottom of page 349. It's 349, page 2 of this document - is voiced by Milan Babic, at the bottom of that page. He justified the round table idea, that is, having a round-table discussion of municipal delegates. 42 of the deputies are of Serbian nationality, which is why he is in favour of the round table, "uniting all our deputies and the left-wing Serbs. That would be Serbs in the two opposition parties. And then taking account to see how many of the Muslim nationals from the Left Bloc we need." And then on the next page, Milan Curcija speaks and says he agrees with the comments but also with the possibility of using money to win their support. Maintained the position that if it did not work, joining the ZOBK, we would break up the municipality and create Prijedor II. The essence of this meeting is a discussion about the unsuccessful attempt of the SDS to bring Prijedor municipality into the ZOBK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, even though at this time Prijedor could not become a member of this association of municipalities, as you've already explained, was there any influence exerted by this regional government of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In summer 1991, there's a document that includes Prijedor within the ZOBK, even though it formally had not joined. In addition, the ZOBK leaders asserted the organisation's jurisdiction over the television relay station on Mount Kozara, at Lisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 19, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, you'll find that document that is relevant to this evidence behind tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is an announcement, is it not, by the assembly -- the community of Bosnia Krajina municipalities, dated 6th August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly state the nature of this announcement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This announcement reports that the presidency of the ZOBK received information that the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina was sending units to take control of the TV relay station at Lisina on Mount Kozara. And then it states that the people of Bosnian Krajina and Pukajza, which would be the area under Mount Kozara, would not allow the intervention of HMUP forces in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this, in essence, supports your opinion that even though Prijedor was not yet a member of the ZOBK, this regional government had started to exert significant influence over the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in the minutes of the 30th of April of 1991 that there was reference to the creation of Prijedor II, of a separate municipality within Prijedor. Was there any historical precedent for that particular idea?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. After the Second World War, the socialist government had realigned the internal organisational structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and made Prijedor into something of a district, under which were numerous local units of government. And at one point, one of these was the Omarska area, which then, under some different name, was considered the equivalent of a municipality. Consequently, at one point, Omarska was a separate organisation from Prijedor, and on this basis and other grounds, the SDS proposed to again create an Omarska municipality by breaking away a series of five local communes from Prijedor and creating a new Omarska municipality. This would have been the 110th municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to the minutes of the meeting of the assembly of the Prijedor SDS of the 3rd of July of 1991, which refers to the SDS proposal of that time to create a separate municipality within Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, on page 374 of the Prijedor SDS document, and I believe we've noted this already, Mr. Momcilo Radanovic makes a recommendation to the Prijedor intellectuals to find a way for a larger area of the former Omarska municipality to separate from the Prijedor municipality and join the Banja Luka region. The Banja Luka region in this context was another name that was frequently used to apply to the ZOBK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, were the areas that were to break away and form this separate municipality predominantly occupied by people of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The five local communities or communes were overwhelmingly Serbian in national composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the referendum ever held?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The referendum was scheduled for the 25th of August, 1991, but at the last minute was cancelled, and the press reports quote SDS leaders as citing inadequate preparation of the populations of those five communes, who had either not been told about the referendum or were not properly prepared for the correct way to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to make it clear and distinguish this referendum from the other referendums we've referred to, this was a local referendum to be held in Prijedor in these -- the locally Serb-dominated communes to create a separate Prijedor municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: A separate Omarska municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can now refer you to Exhibit 22, which is a newspaper article. Now, this newspaper article I think contains comments by Dr. Stakic in respect of that referendum. Could you just state to the Judges what Dr. Stakic had to say about the referendum.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He was interviewed for this article. So the journalist says because the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Cehajic, was on vacation, which makes sense in August, but reaching Dr. Stakic, he told the reporter in a quote at the very bottom -- at the end of this article words that I've quoted in the paper on page 10 in my translation into English. He said: "My view is that the demand for an Omarska municipality is motivated by accumulated problems, but we must bear in mind that an unfavourable moment was selected for the referendum, and it is best to await a more favourable time."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this referendum ever discussed by the Municipal Assembly or the executive committee of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In this article, prior to the quote I've just read, Dr. Stakic is asked if the referendum, or the movement for a separate municipality, was discussed in either the executive committee or the Municipal Assembly, and he indicates that it was never brought to the attention of either body. He does mention some prior discussion last year -- or the previous year, in the Omarska area, about this, but says that nothing recent was discussed by those two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the matter of this particular referendum at this time was never placed before the SDA, the HDZ, or the Left Bloc party, as far as this newspaper article indicates?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think four days after the referendum on the creation of a separate municipality was supposed to take place, a meeting of the SDS deputies club took place in Prijedor. And if I can refer you to the meeting of the 29th of August of 1991, which you will find on page 381 of the SDS Board minutes. And I think that these set of minutes is essentially dealing with a crisis in the leadership and the election of new leaders of the SDS following the failure of this referendum. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you highlight for the Judges the important parts of this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Just to be clear, it took place four days after the scheduled but cancelled referendum and is entitled, "Meeting of the SDS Deputies Club and SDS local board presidents." This meeting, then, is not of the SDS Main Board but of the deputies of the SDS in the Municipal Assembly and the presidents of local boards of the party. And the meeting is opened, in the second paragraph, by Dragan Savanovic, who was the president of the Deputies Club. And in that paragraph it states: "Dragan Savanovic gave the introductory remarks on the reasons for calling the meeting. The reason was that the meeting of the SDS municipal board was not called." Two paragraphs down, Mr. Srdic warned that the Deputies Club could not make the decision. Only the SDS municipal board could do so." And next paragraph, Dragan Savanovic recommended the party's organisational structure. This is the first indication of a totally new organisational scheme for the party's operation: "Only the SDS municipal board could do so." I'm sorry. Wrong quotation. "The deputies club had no intention of taking power." Then down one paragraph, Mr. Srdic: "It is alleged that several of us did not complete the division of power." This again a reference to the slowness of fulfilling the inter-party agreement. And down five lines: "As far as SUP is concerned --" SUP was the old term for police "-- based on the election results, the SDA gets the chief and the commander of the traffic police, while the SDS gets the SJB commander." That would be the commander of the police station. Next paragraph: "Dragan Savanovic then put to the vote the Deputies Club decision. In favour of the Deputies Club decision, 17." And in the next paragraph which begins Savanovic, we see that Srdjo Srdic left the meeting. In the subsequent press report on this meeting, Kozarski Vjesnik states that Srdic was thereby ousted from his position as president of the party is not quite accurate, but what rather happens in the rest of this meeting is that the party makes -- or the Deputies Club makes plans for an election of new officers to be held in the next several days. And at the bottom of the next page, 382, Mr. Radetic says in the second paragraph of his comments: "First the circus with a suspension of the party in January, then the circus with the assembly and Neskovic," Neskovic being the person who had been the overseer of the meeting a month and a half before. On the following page, 383, Dr. Stakic expresses his suggestion on the course of things. It's about one-third down the page on 383: "Believed that the Deputies Club should call a meeting of the municipal board." He recommended that it should say that the meeting was called at the initiative of the Deputies Club in order to call a session of the assembly. And that assembly will turn out to be an electoral assembly of the party to designate new leaders "and that the stamp should be brought to the SDS office." On the following page, 384, halfway down, he speaks again and says: "We should not hurry with the assembly session. It should be prepared." And Savanovic follows by saying: "The municipal board meeting on Tuesday, 3 September 1991, at 1900 hours, and the election assembly meeting on Tuesday, at 1800 hours, is accepted unanimously." The rest of this document is the public statement that the party will make following this meeting, announcing the election assembly. And on the last page, 385, a much more blunt statement for -- if we go to the third line on page 385, only for Sarajevo and Banja Luka. This would be only for the SDS organisation superiors and internal consumption, a very blunt assessment of the party's failures under the outgoing leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Dr. Donia, we can go to the next set of minutes, which Your Honours will find on page 386, and this is a meeting of the 3rd of September of 1991 of the SDS Prijedor municipal board. If you could point out the significant parts of this meeting, please, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This meeting of the SDS Prijedor municipal board, local board chairman and Deputies Club, 3 September 1991, begins with a progress report by Mr. Savanovic, and in the next paragraph after point 1: "A report on a trip made to Sarajevo by five party members:" Savanovic himself, Dr. Stakic, Mr. Vojinovic, as well as Mr. Srdic and Pavic. And in that paragraph, it's clear that the purpose of their trip to Sarajevo was to meet with the party president, Radovan Karadzic, who accepted the organisational structure that was proposed, and that entailed an expansion of the number of members of the municipal board. About two-thirds of the way down the page, Vujinovic clarified the problem of president Karadzic naming ten people in the municipal board. This is the first of a couple of indications that Karadzic insisted on or subsequently appointed these members of the municipal board of the Prijedor SDS. On the next page, 387, the second speaker on that page, Savanovic, says: "Karadzic gave an order to hold municipal board meetings every week. This is one of the ways of addressing the previously perceived weakness of inadequate meetings. Three speakers down, Dr. Stakic says: "Karadzic will take such measures if we do not work well. A proposal to expand the board to include new people with no connection to the local boards. One option is to postpone the assembly session for four Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or five days and prepare everything." And subsequently in this meeting, it -- or subsequently it is agreed by this body that electoral assembly will be deferred until the 11th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Dr. Donia, we could refer to the SDS municipal board and Deputies Club meeting of the 9th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, you will find that on page 392, if you are looking at the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What, if anything, of significance occurred at this meeting, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: At this meeting, which is entitled "SDS municipal board and Deputies Club meeting 9 September 1991," this transitional Working Group, headed by Savanovic, continues its work and determines the list of candidates for the electoral meeting assembly to be held two days later. On page 393, halfway down the page, Mr. Rodic says Srdic, who is the president, is not to be put on the list, by unanimous decision it was concluded that Srdic could not be placed on the list of presidential candidates. This was his final removal from power. However, he -- it should be noted, I think, that he was a remarkably gracious loser. He was a deputy in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and continued to be active and I think quite an important member of the party organisation in Prijedor even after his removal as president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now if we can move to the meeting of the 11th of September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, you will find on page 397.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is a meeting at which a new leadership of the SDS is appointed in Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you highlight from this document the important parts for Their Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This session, entitled, "Minutes of the assembly meeting of the Prijedor municipal organisation of the Serbian Democratic Party," held on 11 September 1991, begins with the nomination of a three-person group to chair this session. Those three persons are Dragan Savanovic, Milomir Stakic, and Milan Pilipovic. This is a very public, open meeting. In fact, people were invited from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it begins with the singing of the national anthem of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and God give us justice anthem. There's a long introductory speech by Professor Pilipovic, which is reported almost, very extensively, in the press article dealing with this meeting. On page 398, item 1, halfway down the page, "adoption of the rules of procedure for the Prijedor SDS municipal organisation assembly." There's a new set of rules of procedure that are being implemented. Three paragraphs down, we see that Radomir Neskovic, the representative of the SDS Main Board who had been present in July is present here as well. He asked to address the assembly. He suggested an addendum to Article 7. And at the bottom of this page, Radomir Neskovic objects to Article 41. So the Sarajevo SDS organisation plays an important role, I think, in this particular meeting. On pages 399 and 400, the results of the voting for the president and vice-president of the party are reported. At the bottom of page 399, the report is made that Mr. Simo Miskovic receives the vast majority of votes, with 121. And on page 400, for vice-president, Dr. Milomir Stakic received 103 votes. Again, the vast majority of votes. And finally, this meeting is closed by three brief addresses at the -- about halfway down the printed portion of this page, one by Mr. Neskovic, another by Professor Cehajic, the SDA leader, president of the Municipal Assembly, and finally, the president of the SDP, which is the Social Democratic Party, Mr. Keric. So at this public meeting, the guests include the leaders of these other parties, who express their -- as a courtesy, express their greetings to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, having reviewed all of these documents and newspaper reports together, after this change in leadership, after the appointment of Miskovic and Dr. Stakic to the leadership of the SDS, how does the style of leadership change?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This election brings an end to most of the contention in the party and results in many discussions that show party members to be focused on specific projects and experiencing substantial successes with the party's work on these individual projects. It's a much more dynamic and focused organisation following the election of September 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think after the election takes place, the party issues a public statement, and you will find that reported in Kozarski Vjesnik. It's Exhibit SK9. And I think you refer in your report to this particular announcement by the party as a demonstration of the change in the style of leadership and relations with other political parties. Could you explain to the Judges the nature of this particular public statement and why it supports your opinion that there was this significant change in the nature of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not quite clear on the -- this is a report on the session of the assembly. This is a statement of I believe the 17th of September by the party, which expresses the party's dissatisfaction with the SDA's performance in the pursuit of the inter-party agreement, and in the second paragraph of the article, on the right-hand side of the exhibit that you have mentioned, charges that at a time when the SDA held this interim appointment of the chief of the police station, that the party, the SDA, used that occasion, with the cooperation of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to smuggle arms into the Muslim-majority village of Kozarac. And this was, of course, an agreement, the division of police portfolios was an agreement that had been reached by the party's previous leadership, but this represents a very different tone in terms of its approach to cooperation or relations with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated a little bit of uncertainty about this. It's actually on page 6 of your report. And I want to direct you to something else that you state on that page. You refer to this statement about the SDA and the BiH colluding in smuggling weapons and then you refer to a statement made the next day by Dr. Stakic. Could you please refer to that statement made by Dr. Stakic and explain the significance of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: On the 18th of September, just one week after the election, Dr. Stakic is quoted as having made a statement at a session of the -- or prior to a session of the executive committee of the municipality, charging that the SDA had violated the inter-party agreement and instead argued that the basis for the inter-party agreement should be the population structure of not just the Prijedor municipality but three adjoining municipalities as well. And that was not carried out in Prijedor; therefore, the SDA had violated the inter-party agreement. And he subsequently, along with Mr. Kovacevic, led a walkout of all SDS members from the executive committee of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I interrupt you just in this point of time, making reference to page 6 of your report. You just mentioned this sentence referring to Dr. Stakic's announcement, and then in your report you have footnote 14, from scientific point of view it's quite clear you have to quote it as you did. But unfortunately, we, the Judges, can't understand this language. Could you please be so kind and translate footnote 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if I read the Serbian, if a translator might go into English or French? And you'll have to forgive -- all of you have to forgive my pronunciation in the language. "[Interpretation] By an agreement between the parties, it is envisaged that the commander of the station should be elected by the majority population. As for his deputy, he should be elected amongst the second-largest community. Since the Serb people in these four municipalities constitutes the majority, then the commander of the public security station should be a Serb. This was not done in Prijedor. Therefore, the SDS is withdrawing its deputies both from the executive board and the assembly of municipalities. The vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Stakic, and Mr. Kovacevic, then left the meeting of the Executive Council."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just to refer back to your prior evidence, this was a very different line than was being taken by Mr. Srdic, the prior president of the SDS in Prijedor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a different approach to the question of the inter-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Srdic had regarded the SDA as having actually complied, by and large, with the inter-party agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that he viewed him as having complied to a point. There remain substantial disagreements. However, he accepted in principle the division of these offices according to the inter-party agreement at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here Dr. Stakic is essentially stating that the Serb population in four municipalities, rather than just Prijedor, should be taken into account in deciding on these positions within the police force?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was that something that was originally envisaged by the inter-party agreement that had been agreed by the national parties after the multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was not foreseen, or a part of those agreements, as we can -- I'm able to identify them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in your report, Dr. Donia, you identify five significant events which took place after Miskovic and Dr. Stakic were appointed to the leadership of the SDS. The first one you've already referred to, which is a different interpretation of the inter-party agreement. Now, can you recall the other four particularly significant events which took place after this change in the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The party engaged in several activities. I think the most significant was the support for mobilisation of Prijedor TO units for the war in Croatia. The plebiscite of the Serbian people of 9 and 10 November, 1991; the establishment of Serbian-only parallel institutions; and the membership in the ZOBK, which in September 1991 was renamed the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or ARK, A-R-K.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's briefly talk about mobilisation of the Territorial Defence forces in Prijedor, and I want to refer to a document from the bundle of documents relating to your report in Brdjanin and Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to refer to the exhibit number, because it's the same exhibit number in this case and will create complete confusion. What I suggest to do is for me to remove it from the file and give it a new exhibit number in this proceeding, if that is acceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the document can be handed to the witness. For the benefit of the Defence, this is part of the bundle of documents that you either have now or will get shortly after this hearing. You have it already. You have it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, what is the significance of this document? And while you're referring to it, because the Judges don't have it in front of them, if you could place it on the ELMO, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is in fact two documents, one of which is a cover sheet, the one we're looking at now, to municipal -- can I get that larger? Let's see. It's from the Command of the Bosnian Krajina volunteer units in Banja Luka, dated 24 August 1991, to the municipal staffs of volunteer units, indicating that enclosed in an essay submitted at the session of the representatives of the municipalities of Bosnian Krajina. The enclosed report, then, or attached report, is an essay or statement entitled "Aims and organisational principles of the volunteer units on the territory of Bosanska Krajina." This document simply indicates that the volunteer forces in the Bosnian Krajina are calling for others to join them because the JNA does not have sufficient forces to do the tasks which these people believe it should be doing, and makes clear that this is an appeal to Serbs to join as volunteers in support of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could refer you, Dr. Donia, to page 14 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if that document could be returned to me and I will, with the agreement of the registry, give it a number.
